candidates.source_body_excerpt: Incoming chief executive Richard Kenyon will lead a review of Lancashire Cricket’s playing operation after joining the club on Monday 5 October. The review will examine the club’s performance structure, staffing, player contracts, resources and funding. It will also look at support for players from the academy through to the first team. Kenyon joins from Nottinghamshire County Cricket Club, where he has been chief executive. He previously spent more than a decade at Everton Football Club. Lancashire said the review would build on a restructure started by outgoing chief executive Daniel Gidney. Kenyon will work alongside Gidney throughout October during the handover. Club chair Dame Sarah Storey said Kenyon would need to assess “what needs to change to improve results, particularly for our men’s side”. Kenyon will be supported during the review by John Abrahams, Mike Watkinson and Sir Clive Lloyd. Do you have a story for us? candidates.source_summary: A monthly group for neurodivergent people, families and carers in Prestwich is marking its first anniversary in September.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A monthly group for neurodivergent people, families and carers in Prestwich is marking its first anniversary in September. Michelle Mackin, a care co-ordinator working with Bury GP Federation and local GP practices, set up Different Minds, One Community after seeing a need for a place where people could find advice and meet others. The group meets at The Woodthorpe on Bury Old Road. Michelle said it brings together support from social prescribing staff and community groups. Dominic Burke, who has experienced severe food anxiety for more than a decade, said attending the group had helped him find support for his health and search for work. “The group has given me somewhere to go and meet other people in smaller groups, know I will be supported, and get advice,” he said. He has also taken part in activities at Prestwich’s Creative Living Centre and received CV guidance. Maxine Ackerley, a parent of neurodivergent children, said meeting other parents and carers had helped her share experiences and find advice. “This group gives you somewhere to come and be heard and helped,” she said. Different Minds, One Community meets on the second Wednesday of each month from 1.30pm to 3pm at The Woodthorpe, Bury Old Road, Prestwich M25 0EG. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Members and volunteers at The Bread and Butter Thing’s Matthew Moss food club celebrated the charity’s 10th anniversary. The Rochdale club was one of more than 160 hubs across England to mark the anniversary. Members and volunteers gathered for cake and a brew. The club offers three bags of food, including fruit and vegetables, chilled items and cupboard staples, from £8.50. Members can also meet neighbours and volunteer at the weekly hub. The Bread and Butter Thing began with a hired van delivering surplus food to a community centre in Moss Side, Manchester. The charity says it now supports more than 100,000 households through hubs in more than 160 communities. Vic Harper, the charity’s chief executive, said: “People knowing they can rely on us, week after week. That’s only possible because of the incredible members, volunteers and partners who make hubs like Matthew Moss such an important part of their community.” Do you have a story for us? candidates.source_summary: A campaign has been launched to keep children safe by reminding drivers they have to stop for school crossing patrols.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A campaign has been launched to keep children safe by reminding drivers they have to stop for school crossing patrols. The drive was launched last week at St Luke’s Primary School in Heywood. As well as getting across the Stop Means Stop message, parking wardens will be on patrol outside schools to enforce restrictions. Rochdale Council shared: “We know that life is busy and we all need to get to places fast, but now the kids are back in school, it’s more important than ever that we take it slow and leave space around schools. “There were 137 fail to stops outside schools over the past five years, with people driving straight through, even after our school crossing patrols had stepped into the road. Cllr Dylan Williams launches the Stop Means Stop campaign at St Luke’s Primary School in Heywood. Image: Rochdale Council “People also continue to park on lines outside schools, significantly reducing visibility and increasing the likelihood that a child could get hurt. “Cllr Dylan Williams, our cabinet member for Highways and Facilities launched the Stop Means Stop campaign for our borough at St Luke’s in Heywood and also announced parking enforcement patrols are being massively increased around schools to help combat the issue.

candidates.source_summary: Greater Manchester Police have launched a full murder investigation following the discovery of a 44-year-old woman found deceased at an address on Tweedale Street in Rochdale on 25 May 2026.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Greater Manchester Police officers attended an address on Tweedale Street in Rochdale at approximately 4 p.m. on Monday, 25 May 2026, following reports of a concern for welfare. Officers discovering the 44-year-old woman deceased at the scene initiated immediate contact with ambulance services, though medical personnel could only confirm the victim’s death rather than undertake resuscitative measures. The initial incident classification reflected uncertainty regarding the cause of death, with responding officers treating the circumstances as potentially suspicious rather than immediately declaring murder investigation protocols. However, subsequent examination and preliminary forensic assessment rapidly escalated the investigation to full murder inquiry status. Detective senior investigating officers commenced immediate containment procedures, establishing crime scene security and preserving evidence for later forensic examination. Specialist teams from Greater Manchester Police’s Major Incident Team assumed investigative responsibilities, utilising established protocols for homicide inquiries. Kyle Howard, aged 25 years old and residing at the same Tweedale Street property where the victim was discovered, was arrested on suspicion of murder within hours of the police response. Howard’s presence at the address and circumstantial evidence established through immediate neighbourhood canvassing and witness interviews accelerated suspect identification significantly. By 3 June 2026, eight days following the initial discovery, Greater Manchester Police confirmed that Howard had been charged with murder and remanded in custody pending court proceedings. His appearance at Manchester Magistrates Court on 3 June 2026 formalised the charge, with the defendant remanded in custody pending further court appearances and trial preparation. Greater Manchester Police characterised the investigation as complete regarding the immediate arrest phase, though ongoing inquiries continued regarding potential additional circumstances or contributing factors surrounding the death. Greater Manchester Police’s Major Incident Team operates structured investigative frameworks encompassing witness identification, forensic evidence preservation, and secure evidence chain management. Following death notification to next of kin, supported by specialist family liaison officers, investigators establish timeline reconstructions, witness statement gathering, and preliminary forensic assessment protocols. Detective Chief Inspector Liz Hopkinson, of Greater Manchester Police’s Major Incident Team, told investigators that “this is a tragic set of circumstances where a woman has lost her life, and we have a team of dedicated officers working around the clock to establish what happened.” The characterisation reflects the emotional gravity of homicide investigations whilst emphasising systematic investigative commitment.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Vale of Lune’s winning streak continued as they kicked off the new season with Saturday’s 32-28 victory at Rochdale, writes BARRY LEES. The first XV’s first meaningful encounter of the NW1 adventure had seen livewire flanker Sam Walton leave early for treatment to an eye injury. Reorganising ensued and the skill set of the crew on the bench began to kick in. Rochdale stepped up production and pressed into the Vale 22, where they powered over the tryline to open the scoring. Together, the two organisations raised £7,875.52. The Trust says Changing Lives has supported 33 people in its first eight months. It offers free football alongside wellbeing, personal development and employability activities. Its aim is to give participants a place to meet others, improve their physical and mental wellbeing, and find routes into volunteering, education or work. During those eight months, the programme has held 28 football and engagement sessions, five specialist workshops and four free haircut sessions. Participants have played two competitive football fixtures and attended two Rochdale AFC first-team matches. When the partnership was announced in December 2025, Scott Webster, the Trust’s deputy director, said it would give people “the chance to improve their health and well-being, develop a sense of community and belonging, and gain valuable skills for future progression.” This year’s sleep out invites individuals, families, businesses, schools and community groups to spend a night under the floodlights at the Crown Oil Arena. People can join on their own or as part of a group. Those unable to take part can donate. The Trust says the event is intended to support people affected by homelessness, rather than recreate their experience. Money raised will help continue Changing Lives and offer its activities to more people. People can sign up or donate through the event page .

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Ten-man Rochdale survived a Fleetwood onslaught to earn a 2-1 victory at Highbury. The visitors raced into a two-goal lead inside 14 minutes, Dajaune Brown netting with a first-time finish from Glenn Middleton’s cross in the eighth minute before Aden Flint doubled Dale’s advantage, coolly slotting home after Brown’s shot fell kindly into his path. Mark Helm hit back on the half-hour mark, pouncing on a loose ball in midfield and finishing neatly into the bottom corner. Fleetwood pushed hard for an equaliser, with Ched Evans’ shot deflected inches wide, Raffaele Cirino hitting the side-netting and Aaron Loupalo-Bi narrowly wide with a fierce low drive. The home side dominated the second half but Lewis McCann clearing the bar by inches was as close as they got. Dale’s task got even tougher on 69 minutes when Tobi Adebayo-Rowling received a second yellow card for a shirt pull. Goalkeeper Sam Waller then denied Evans and Flint got his head to Ronan Coughlan’s goalbound shot as valiant defending, and Fleetwood’s wayward finishing, saw Dale hold on for the win.

candidates.source_summary: A Middleton woman who stopped drinking in 2019 says writing horror stories has helped her explore her experiences of addiction and trauma.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A Middleton woman who stopped drinking in 2019 says writing horror stories has helped her explore her experiences of addiction and trauma. Alex Herod said she tried meetings, therapy, books and sober communities before she began writing fiction as part of her recovery. She has a diagnosis of complex PTSD and is now working on a creative writing PhD about the role horror writing plays in her own recovery. “Although I write fiction, most of my stories relate back to themes of addiction, trauma, mental health, transformation and recovery,” she said. “Writing horror has allowed me to go into very dark places and come out the other side. I can explore feelings of disgust and monstrousness - how I felt about myself when I was drinking, or how I felt others saw me - and do so in a way that is in my control.” Alex said being able to edit and rewrite a story gives her a way to express experiences she previously felt unable to discuss. She described the process as “making friends with my monsters”. “It helps me to process my experiences of addiction and trauma, and learn to accept and embrace the darker parts of myself so I don’t feel disconnected,” she said. Alex, who works at the University of Salford, is due to release her debut novel next year. candidates.source_summary: Ian Watson lauds Rochdale ‘courage’ after battling win at Fleetwood peeblesshirenews.com
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale manager Ian Watson believes his side showed their mettle in the 2-1 win at Fleetwood. Goals from Dajaune Brown and Aden Flint put Dale 2-0 up early on but they were forced into sterling rearguard action in the second half, especially after Tobi Adebayo-Rowling saw a second yellow card 21 minutes from time, with Mark Helm having reduced the deficit. Watson, who had come under fire during Dale’s slow start to the season, said: “That’s what we want to look like all the time. “I’m just really pleased we get to see what we’re actually working on, what we’re trying to look like, and how brave the boys were with the ball, how much courage they played with. “When they do that, it’s really hard for the opposition. I felt the first 20 was really pleasing, then I think we maybe played the scoreboard a little bit after that and self-preservation mode kicked in a little bit. “We got to half-time and I thought we regrouped, and started the second half really well. There’s so much I love about today’s performance, not just with the ball, but everything without the ball, and the heart and desire the boys showed as well. “I understand where the frustration comes from but my responsibility is to not listen to any noise, just focus and back myself as a coach, as a human as well. My mentality is strong and I believe in myself. But how amazing were the fans as well, they got us over the line.” Fleetwood manager Matt Lawlor cut a frustrated figure having seen his side start slowly and then fail to break Dale down for an equaliser.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Libraries across the borough are teaming up with a local charity to help families make use of thousands of free pre-loved school uniforms and shoes. As families continue to manage the high costs of school uniform, there is growing demand for affordable alternatives, including a reliance on local charities like Uniform For All, which Rochdale Council is working with to support those who need extra help. Every day high-quality pre-loved items, including polo shirts, skirts, trousers, branded school blazers, coats and pumps, are given to families through the charity. Not every family has the resources to travel long distances to collect their orders and the borough’s library service is helping to collect these items so families can pick them up closer to where they live at their nearest library and save on additional travel costs. When residents come in to collect their orders, library staff are also on hand to provide them with additional cost-of-living information and related support, if they need it, alongside free wifi and computer access and other benefits linked to a free library membership. Cllr Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation, said: “We are proud to be supporting this valuable charity in distributing much-needed uniforms to our local families. “Sadly, we know demand is growing for these items so by utilising our libraries, we can help families access what they need within their communities.” Operating since 2020, Uniform For All currently provides more than 20,000 items to more than 3,000 families each year.

Diamond will provide places for three children with complex needs and disabilities who come into care. The opening means 12 placements are now available across the four new council-run homes. The other homes are called Emerald, Sapphire and Ruby, with the jewel-themed names suggested by cared for children. Diamond includes a dedicated sensory room and will have staff on site 24 hours a day. The council said the new provision will allow more children and young people to remain in the borough rather than being placed elsewhere because suitable placements are unavailable locally. Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children's services and education, said: “As the latest jewel in our crown of new homes, I’m delighted to see Diamond open its doors and its homely and friendly feel will make a real difference to the lives of children and young people who need our support. “Our investment into homes like this means more children can receive high-quality care in the areas that they are familiar with and help them to maintain the important relationships and connections which support their wellbeing and development.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Originally posted on June 2, 2023 @ 09:15 Health leaders from Rochdale, Greater Manchester, have shared the success of their collaborative working model with more than 1,000 delegates at a conference in Belgium. Dr Salman Shahid, Associate Medical Director of the Greater Manchester Integrated Care Board, along with a team from One Rochdale Health and Care, presented their integrated approach to healthcare, focusing on improving the well-being of individuals in Rochdale and the wider Greater Manchester region at the International Conference on Integrated Care in Antwerp. During the conference, Dr Kirsty Marshall, Dr Shona McCallum, and Alison Kelly highlighted their work on enhancing patient and public involvement in health and social care services within the region. Dr Shahid, together with Sandra Crossdale and Andrew Hulcoop, took to the stage to discuss the “Integration Continuum” and its significance in achieving patient-centered care within an integrated healthcare model. “Our attendance at this conference aimed to foster learning and exchange experiences regarding the challenges faced by modern healthcare systems,” said Dr Shahid. “We showcased how hospitals, community services, GP practices, voluntary organizations, as well as educational and research teams, collaborate to deliver integrated healthcare, putting patients at the center of care.” He added, “This conference provided an excellent opportunity for us to gain insights from colleagues across Europe and further enhance our approaches and systems, ultimately creating a better health and social care system for our residents.” Rochdale is among the ten areas in Greater Manchester with significant health and care inequalities. Dr Shahid emphasized the need for a multi-disciplinary approach and recognition of all contributors, including voluntary, research, and education sectors, in tackling long-term medical conditions. By prioritizing better integration, the aim is to achieve a seamless health and well-being model with shared responsibility for patient care.

But, as the gaffer and captain said after the game, they didn’t. Conceding an early goal to defensive lapses was a sickener and knocked the wind out of us straightaway but to play as poorly as we did, yet still miss a hatful of clear cut chances which should have seen us handsomely in the lead at the interval, made everything even worse. I’ve never seen a worse miss in person than that of Mike Fondop when he managed to entirely miss the gaping open goal in front of him, and Kane Drummond was also guilty of a poor miss, making a mess of the rebound from his own original saved effort, with the goal at his mercy. Just as at Tranmere, Kavanagh appeared for the second half but, really, we did very little else other than huff and puff with only a Fondop header hitting the post near the death to show for it. Even going 2-0 down after more defensive errors didn’t serve to push us on and the most worrying aspect of the whole game was the lack of urgency and togetherness on display. I mentioned last week something doesn’t seem quite right in the camp and I stand by that. Even Ollie Norburn said performance levels haven’t been good in September but he wasn’t sure why.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: RivingtonHark, on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council, has secured British clothing retailer Peacocks on a long-term lease for a 10,181 sq ft unit at Rochdale Riverside, taking the scheme to 92% occupancy. The run of new lettings follows a 15.3% year-on-year footfall increase at Rochdale Riverside, with almost 200,000 visiting during July, continuing an upward year-on-year trend throughout 2026. Following its opening in Spring 2020, Rochdale Riverside has delivered a dynamic mix of shopping, dining, and leisure and is at the heart of the wider regeneration of Rochdale town centre. RivingtonHark has asset managed the centre on behalf of the council since 2023. The 200,000sq ft open-air scheme is anchored by a 50,000sq ft M&S store and a six-screen Real Cinema, and is home to leading national retailers including Next, H&M, Boots, and JD Sports. Ollie Holland, asset manager for Rochdale Riverside at RivingtonHark, said: “The letting brings another nationally recognised retailer to Rochdale Riverside, activating a prominent, centrally located unit and further strengthening the diverse and growing fashion offer. The addition of Peacocks reflects robust demand for well situated space and continued confidence from national and regional occupiers in the long-term appeal of Rochdale Riverside. “Rochdale Riverside is another example of how we work closely with local authorities like Rochdale Borough Council to deliver long-term value across town and city centre schemes. With footfall continuing to grow and further lettings in the pipeline we look forward to building on this continued momentum.” Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for regeneration and housing at Rochdale Borough Council, said: “It’s great to see Rochdale Riverside going from strength to strength with another new store signing up. I’m sure Peacocks will prove to be a popular addition to this busy and well-loved shopping and leisure centre.” Established in Warrington in 1884 and now trading from 345 stores nationally, Peacocks brings a budget friendly, everyday proposition which adds to the diverse retail mix. Peacocks is scheduled to open at the start of October and will trade across both ground and first floor levels.

candidates.source_summary: Pioneering digital autopsies could cut the need for invasive post-mortems by up to 80 per cent, reducing the distress caused to grieving loved ones.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Pioneering digital autopsies could cut the need for invasive post-mortems by up to 80 per cent, reducing the distress caused to grieving loved ones. The innovative service is being delivered by the Coroner’s Office for Greater Manchester, in partnership with the NHS, specialist post-mortem imaging provider Anubix, and medical imaging provider TIC Health. Working with pathologists, radiologists and mortuary staff at the Northern Care Alliance the coroner’s office will, where appropriate, provide computed tomography (CT) scanning to help inform a person’s cause of death. Teams will use post-mortem imaging to check if a cause of death can be determined without the need for traditional invasive post-mortems, a process that can cause further distress to relatives during the grieving process across Rochdale, Bury, and Oldham. A number of scans a week will be carried out using the new technology, with a long-term ambition of speeding up the service provided for relatives following the loss of a loved one. Cllr Neil Emmott, leader of Rochdale Council, said: “This is a highly sensitive issue that has been carefully handled. “Working in partnership across the health sector, this will help to futureproof the coroner’s service and ensure families and loved ones continue to get the best possible support. “I know from speaking with residents across Heywood, Middleton, Pennines and Rochdale how invasive post-mortems often causes additional anxiety at a time of grief, so this is a timely and welcome new service.”
